title: Work and Family – A Balancing Act

paragraphs.text: Gilchrist (1991) noted that following significant social change during the last thirty years, the nuclear family with one working parent is no longer the norm in many parts of the world. Glezer (1991) points out that traditional household roles, with the man being the breadwinner and the wife staying at home to look after the house and children, have been changing for years.

Women are increasingly working in the paid workforce (Carmody 1990) and in countries such as Australia, 53% of married women were working for pay in 1990 (Wolcott 1992). The increased numbers of women in the workplace have given many a stronger voice to demand benefits that will help to balance work and family responsibilities.

Wolcott (1992) suggests that excessive work hours, rigid work schedules and fatigue contribute to work and family conflict. Edgar (1991) believes that the rigidities of workplace awards and practices are major contributors to family stress, conflict and breakdown and recommendations by Smith (1992) suggest that more needs to be done by managers at individual workplaces via consultation with individual employees and trade unions to break down rigidities.

The most frequently discussed solution is to provide flexibility. A number of authors (Love 1987; Viveros-Long 1981) suggest that this flexibility should be of a reciprocal nature between the employer and the employee and that a more open-minded and innovative approach to the structure of work is required. 'Caregivers on Call', a New York-based 24-hour service that arranges to have appropriate and qualified caregivers to fill in during emergencies as well as to provide on-site temporary childcare for school holidays, is often cited as an appropriate example. Other countries, such as Sweden and Belgium, have introduced paid family leave and tax concessions to assist workers with family responsibilities.

Australian organisations that have family-friendly work practices generally report that they have reduced absenteeism, decreased staff turnover and increased productivity (Lee 1991). Results from a survey in the United States in 1991 asking managers to list the benefits of family-friendly work practices, showed an increase in morale (35%), easier recruitment (32%) and improved employee retention (26%) as the top three benefits.

This study reports on work practices in Australia. Human resource managers were surveyed concerning family-friendly practices in their organisations to discover whether: • Australian organisations were family-friendly; • respondent organisations' top management believed the responsibility for providing a family-friendly workplace should be equally shared between the government, the employer and the employee; • family-friendly organisations reported organisational benefits as a result of having implemented family-friendly work practices.

There were 72 respondents to the study, of whom 65% were female. Human resource managers were randomly selected across Australia from a wide cross-section of industries of varying organisational sizes.

Respondents were asked to indicate how important certain factors in their organisation were in deciding to implement family-friendly work practices. A number of factors were considered to be important with changes in social values regarding the roles of men and women at work and at home, and the increase in the number of women in the paid workforce, considered to be the most important.

When asked 'How does your organisation's top management believe the responsibility of assisting employees to manage their work and family conflict should be apportioned?', two thirds of respondents said tht the individual should be largely responsible.

75% of respondents considered organisations to be moderately or extremely family-friendly.The majority of respondent organisations had in fact implemented a number of family-friendly work practices with part-time work, shorter hours and relocation assistance being the most common. For those organisations that did not provide the listed family-friendly work practices, the major reasons cited were: • no employee demand – 38% • not practical to implement – 16.9% • not considered to be an issue – 9.8% • cost prohibitive – 8.9% The majority of respondents perceived their organisation had gained benefits from introducing family-friendly work practices, with 45% reporting increased employee job satisfaction. However, when asked how many organisations actually evaluated their family-friendly work initiatives, only 34.7% stated that they did. A major difficulty in the evaluation process is that it is sometimes unclear as to which outcomes were caused by family-friendly work practices and which by other factors that may have changed at the same time.

Organisations need to meet the changing needs of the workforce in an environment where family-friendly work practices are perceived as luxuries by organisations, they have become a necessity in Australian society today where, in 56% of two-parent families, both parents work. Organisations in this study that have implemented family-friendly work practices reported organisational and employee benefits including decreased absenteeism and increased levels of morale. Organisations that adopt a proactive approach regarding the issue of work and family enable their employees to lead less stressful and more productive work and home lives, resulting in benefits to individuals, organisations and to the community at large.
